name: Obagi Blue Peel

card.summary: A branded, standardized TCA medium-depth peel with a thin published record.
card.note: Evidence is limited to a procedure description and small comparisons.

quick.overview:
The Obagi Blue Peel is a branded TCA-based medium peel. A 1999 paper described it as a standardized method with depth control.

Few studies exist beyond that and a hand-rejuvenation comparison.
quick.mechanism: TCA causes controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis, after which skin sheds and renews.
quick.risks: Medium peels carry risks of pigment change, prolonged redness and scarring.

lead: The Obagi Blue Peel is a branded trichloroacetic acid (TCA) chemical peel performed in a clinic to improve skin texture, tone and signs of sun damage. A 1999 Dermatologic Surgery paper described it as a standardized TCA-based procedure intended to sit between superficial exfoliating peels and a classic medium-depth peel, with depth judged from clinical signs and a blue colour guide that helps even application.[1]

People seek peels like this to even out blotchy pigmentation, soften fine lines and refine rough, sun-damaged skin so the face looks smoother and fresher. DermNet describes TCA peels in general as treating photoageing, pigmentation, freckles and texture, with fine wrinkles and some acne scars becoming less obvious.[6]

Published studies of the Blue Peel itself are few: the 1999 procedure paper, a 2002 comparison of Er:YAG laser and Blue Peel for photoaged hands,[2] a 2006 paper on performing the peel faster and less expensively,[3] and a 2000 letter commenting on the technique.[4]

chain: TCA solution applied to the face in a controlled coating
Top layers of skin shed over about a week
Smoother, more even-toned skin as new skin forms
angle.text: A Blue Peel is applied by a clinician to remove damaged outer skin layers, which people use to reduce sun-related blotchiness, fine lines and uneven texture. The coloured base lets the practitioner see where solution has been applied.

paras: The 1999 paper described a coating system for TCA application: the peel solution is a mix of TCA and a commercial base, and its colour acts as a guide to even application and to avoiding skipped areas. The authors aimed to simplify and standardize TCA peeling, to define depth from intraoperative clinical signs, and to reduce variables that cause inconsistent results, noting that TCA peel outcomes otherwise vary with physician skill, patient selection and patient management.[1] The abstract places the technique in the context of TCA peels at concentrations ranging from 30% to 50%.[1]

A 2006 Skinmed paper describes the Obagi Blue Peel as a well-accepted and popular method worldwide, prepared by mixing a fixed volume of 30% TCA with the Blue Peel base. The authors propose modifications for faster, cheaper performance, including preparing larger batches, using higher concentrations to reduce the number of coats, and storing prepared solution for at least a year.[3]

DermNet describes TCA as a medium-depth peel, usually performed by a dermatologist or plastic surgeon. The procedure is described as painful, with skin remaining swollen, red and crusted for about a week and mild redness lasting several weeks; most people take around a week off work, and moderate-depth peels are usually repeated no sooner than 3 to 6 months.[6] Wikipedia says patients often feel warmth or burning and may receive a tranquilizer with an oral pain reliever.[5]

Patients are typically prepared with nightly creams for several weeks beforehand, such as tretinoin, an alpha hydroxy acid or hydroquinone, and are advised to use broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen, especially in the first six months after the peel.[6]

Possible complications of TCA peels include blocked pores or acne, bacterial, yeast or herpes infection, scarring from infection or picking, and blotchy pigmentation.[6] Wikipedia lists photosensitivity, lingering redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning and texture changes, and notes that the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise.[5]

DermNet reports TCA peels are most often used on fair skin (Fitzpatrick types I to III), whereas people with darker skin (types IV to VI) face higher risks of pigment change and scarring, so lighter peels are generally chosen.[6]

Chemical peeling is traced to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid to treat freckles and skin irregularities; phenol-croton oil peels entered mainstream practice in the 1960s.[5] The Blue Peel was described in the dermatology literature in 1999, and by 2006 was characterised as popular worldwide.[1][3]

The 1999 report presented a standardized procedure rather than a controlled trial.[1] A 2002 comparative study examined edema, erythema, temperature and re-epithelialization after Er:YAG laser versus Blue Peel on the hands of 22 patients with photoaging, with 3 months of follow-up; early postoperative edema, erythema and temperature were more intense in the laser group, but the groups became similar over time.[2] A 2000 letter in Dermatologic Surgery commented on the technique.[4] No large randomized trials of the Blue Peel for the face were found.
